questions.title: Process that forms the spinal cord
questions.question: Formation of the spinal cord is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Folding describes the embryo's overall shape change from a flat disc into a cylindrical body, a separate process from the specific formation of the neural tube.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fertilization is the union of sperm and oocyte at the very start of development, weeks before the neural tube exists.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Implantation is the embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium, an even earlier event than fertilization's neural consequences.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrulation is the process that forms the three germ layers; it precedes and sets up neurulation but is not itself the formation of the spinal cord.
explanations.E: Correct. Neurulation is the process by which the ectodermal neural plate folds into the neural tube, which then differentiates into the brain and spinal cord. Fusion of the neural folds begins in the middle of the embryo and spreads towards both ends, closing the tube. This is the specific developmental process the question is naming.

questions.learning_objective: Name neurulation as the process that folds the neural plate into the neural tube, forming the CNS.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Lower part of the brainstem
questions.question: The lower part of the brainstem is called:

explanations.A: Correct. The medulla oblongata is the lowest of the brainstem's three parts, continuous below with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. It sits beneath the pons in the bottom-to-top order medulla, pons, midbrain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The midbrain is the highest part of the brainstem, continuous above with the diencephalon and cerebrum, the opposite end from the one this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pons is the middle part of the brainstem, lying between the medulla below and the midbrain above, not the lowest part.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebellum is attached to the back of the brainstem by the cerebellar peduncles but is not itself one of the brainstem's three named parts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The diencephalon lies above the midbrain, at the top of the brainstem's neighbouring structures, not at the brainstem's lower end.

questions.learning_objective: State that the medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Cells that synthesize myelin in the peripheral nervous system
questions.question: Which of the following cells synthesize myelin in the peripheral nervous system?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microglia are the CNS's resident phagocytes and immune cells; they do not produce myelin anywhere in the nervous system.
explanations.B: Correct. Schwann cells wrap around peripheral axons and produce the myelin sheath along the length of a peripheral nerve fibre. One Schwann cell myelinates a single internode of a single axon, unlike the CNS's oligodendrocytes, which myelinate segments of several different axons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ependymal cells line the CSF-filled ventricles and central canal; they play no part in myelin production.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Astrocytes support neurons metabolically and help form the blood-brain barrier in the CNS, but they do not produce myelin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Oligodendrocytes are the CNS's myelinating cell, the central counterpart to the peripheral Schwann cell asked for here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Schwann cells as the myelinating cell of the peripheral nervous system.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Functional unit of the nervous system
questions.question: The functional unit of the nervous system is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The astrocyte is a supporting glial cell, not the cell that performs the nervous system's own tasks of receiving, conducting and transmitting impulses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The oligodendrocyte is a myelinating glial cell of the CNS, again a support cell rather than the functional unit itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system: every task the nervous system performs is carried out by neurons acting alone or in circuits. Glial cells such as those in the other options support and insulate neurons but do not themselves generate or conduct nerve impulses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Microglia are the CNS's resident phagocytes, an immune support role rather than the functional unit that conducts impulses.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons, a supporting role rather than the impulse-conducting functional unit itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the neuron, not a glial cell, as the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Location of pseudounipolar nerve cells
questions.question: Pseudounipolar nerve cells are present in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sense organs contain a variety of receptor and sensory cell types, but the pseudounipolar shape specifically names spinal and cranial sensory ganglion cells, not sense organs generally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cerebellum's characteristic neuron is the multipolar Purkinje cell, not a pseudounipolar cell.
explanations.C: Correct. Spinal and cranial sensory ganglion cells, including those of the dorsal root ganglia, have a single process leaving the cell body. That single process divides at once into two branches, which is why these cells are described as pseudounipolar rather than truly unipolar. This makes the dorsal root ganglion the standard location taught for this neuron shape.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebral cortex is dominated by multipolar neurons, cells with one axon and many dendrites, not pseudounipolar cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The retina's bipolar cells, which relay signals from photoreceptors to ganglion cells, have two processes rather than the single, later-dividing process of a pseudounipolar cell.

questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > CNS / Nervous System
questions.learning_objective: Locate pseudounipolar neurons in the dorsal root (and cranial sensory) ganglia.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Upper part of the brainstem
questions.question: The upper part of the brainstem is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pons is the middle part of the brainstem, sitting between the medulla below and the midbrain above.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medulla is the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord, the opposite end from the one this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thalamus is part of the diencephalon, which sits above the midbrain, and is not itself one of the brainstem's three named parts.
explanations.D: Correct. The midbrain is the highest of the brainstem's three parts, continuous above with the diencephalon and cerebrum. It sits above the pons in the bottom-to-top order medulla, pons, midbrain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The hypothalamus, like the thalamus, is part of the diencephalon rather than the brainstem itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the midbrain is the highest part of the brainstem.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: Cavity of the cerebral hemisphere
questions.question: The lateral ventricle is the cavity of the:

explanations.A: Correct. Each cerebral hemisphere contains one lateral ventricle. It is a C-shaped, CSF-filled cavity, and it is the largest of the brain's four ventricles. The other three ventricles belong instead to the diencephalon, midbrain and hindbrain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diencephalon's cavity is the third ventricle, a separate, single midline ventricle, not the paired lateral ventricles asked about here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The midbrain's cavity is the narrow cerebral aqueduct, connecting the third and fourth ventricles, not the lateral ventricle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hindbrain's cavity is the fourth ventricle, lying between the pons/medulla and the cerebellum, distinct from the lateral ventricle of the cerebral hemisphere.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The spinal cord's cavity is the central canal, a narrow continuation of the ventricular system, not the lateral ventricle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral ventricle is the cavity contained within each cerebral hemisphere.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.title: How spinal nerves are formed
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the spinal nerves is correct?

options.B: Are formed by union of ventral and dorsal rami
options.C: Are formed by union of ventral and dorsal roots
options.D: Loss of sensation results from injury of the ventral root
options.E: Their number equals the number of the vertebrae

explanations.A: Incorrect. There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves, not 12; twelve is instead the number of thoracic segments and, separately, the number of cranial nerve pairs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal and ventral rami are the two branches a spinal nerve divides into after it has already formed, just outside the vertebral canal, not the structures whose union forms the nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. Each spinal nerve forms, within the vertebral canal, from the union of a dorsal (sensory) root and a ventral (motor) root. Once united, the resulting nerve trunk is mixed, carrying both sensory and motor fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Injury to the ventral root, which carries motor fibres, causes loss of movement, not loss of sensation; sensory loss instead follows injury to the dorsal root.
explanations.E: Incorrect. There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves but only 33 vertebrae grouped into five regions with mismatched segment counts, most notably 8 cervical spinal nerve pairs against only 7 cervical vertebrae, so the two counts do not match.

questions.learning_objective: State that a spinal nerve forms from the union of a dorsal root and a ventral root.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.23

questions.author_notes: Original wording is presented as a stem-plus-completions list ("The spinal nerves: ..."); rephrased into a single question stem for clarity, meaning preserved.

questions.title: Number of cervical spinal nerves
questions.question: The number of the cervical spinal nerves is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Four is not the count for any spinal-cord region; the closest matching count, four, does not correspond to the cervical segments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Six is not one of the spinal cord's regional segment counts (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).
explanations.C: Correct. There are 8 cervical spinal nerve pairs. This is one more than the 7 cervical vertebrae, because the first cervical nerve exits above the first cervical vertebra and the eighth exits below the seventh. Every other spinal region below the neck has a nerve count that matches its vertebral count exactly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ten is not one of the spinal cord's regional segment counts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Twelve is the count of thoracic spinal nerve pairs, not cervical ones.

questions.learning_objective: State that there are 8 pairs of cervical spinal nerves, one more than the 7 cervical vertebrae.

questions.title: Origin of the parasympathetic system
questions.question: Which of the following is true of the parasympathetic system?

options.C: Arises from the thoracic segments of the spinal cord
options.D: Arises from S2, 3 & 4 spinal cord segments

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increasing the heart rate is a sympathetic effect; parasympathetic activity instead slows the heart rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dilating the bronchi (bronchodilatation) is a sympathetic effect; parasympathetic activity instead produces bronchoconstriction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thoracic (and upper two lumbar) spinal cord segments are the sympathetic outflow's origin, not the parasympathetic system's.
explanations.D: Correct. The parasympathetic system has a craniosacral outflow. Preganglionic fibres leave the CNS from the brainstem (the cranial outflow) and separately from the second, third and fourth sacral spinal cord segments (the sacral outflow). At sacral level, the spinal cord's lateral horn carries these preganglionic cell bodies.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The parasympathetic system does have a cranial outflow, carried by cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, alongside its separate sacral outflow.

questions.learning_objective: State that the parasympathetic sacral outflow arises from spinal cord segments S2, S3 and S4.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.24

questions.title: Nerves carrying impulses from the brain to the muscles
questions.question: Which of the following nerves carry impulses from the brain to the muscles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A mixed nerve carries both motor and sensory fibres together; the question specifically asks for the component travelling in the brain-to-muscle direction, which is the motor fibres, not the mixed nerve as a whole.
explanations.B: Correct. Motor (efferent) nerves carry impulses away from the brain and spinal cord out to muscles and glands, producing movement or secretion. This is the direction named in the question, from the CNS towards the muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interneurons are relay neurons that connect other neurons within the CNS itself; they do not form the peripheral nerves that reach out to muscles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sensory (afferent) nerves carry impulses in the opposite direction, from peripheral receptors into the CNS, not from the brain to a muscle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify motor (efferent) nerves as those carrying impulses from the CNS to muscles.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.24

questions.author_notes: Source prints only four options (A-D) for this item; authored as printed rather than padded to five, per the lane's <4-held / >5-trimmed rule (four options is neither).

questions.title: Effect of cerebellar disease
questions.question: Diseases of the cerebellum usually cause:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Paralysis points to a lesion of the corticospinal tract or a lower motor neuron, pathways the cerebellum does not itself carry.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Loss of sensation points to a lesion of a sensory pathway, not the cerebellum, which coordinates movement rather than carrying sensory information to consciousness.
explanations.C: Correct. The cerebellum maintains equilibrium, coordinates the timing and force of voluntary muscle movement, and regulates muscle tone. Because it does not itself initiate movement or carry the sensory or motor pathways, its disease characteristically produces loss of balance and coordination (ataxia) rather than weakness or numbness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Loss of memory points to disease of the cerebral cortex or limbic structures, not the cerebellum.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Loss of vision points to disease of the visual pathway or occipital cortex, not the cerebellum.

questions.learning_objective: State that cerebellar disease characteristically produces loss of balance, not paralysis, sensory loss or memory loss.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.24

questions.title: Aim of an axillary nerve block before wrist surgery
questions.question: A surgeon wished to carry out an operation on a patient's wrist. A local anaesthetic drug was injected into the axilla. The aim of the technique was to:

options.C: Block the spinal nerves of the upper limb
options.D: Produce permanent loss of sensation from the upper limb
options.E: Produce loss of movement of the muscles without affecting the sensation

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal nerve roots lie inside the vertebral canal, far proximal to the axilla; an axillary injection cannot reach structures that far centrally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ventral nerve roots likewise lie inside the vertebral canal, out of reach of an axillary injection.
explanations.C: Correct. The brachial plexus, formed from the ventral rami of spinal nerves C5-T1, passes through the axilla alongside the axillary artery. An axillary block deposits local anaesthetic around this already-formed, mixed peripheral nerve supply of the upper limb, blocking the spinal nerves at that peripheral point.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A local anaesthetic block is temporary, wearing off as the drug is cleared, not a permanent loss of sensation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Because the blocked nerves are mixed (carrying both sensory and motor fibres), the block affects both sensation and movement together, not movement alone while sparing sensation.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that an axillary block anaesthetises the peripheral spinal nerves of the upper limb, not the nerve roots.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.24

questions.title: CSF-filled cavities inside the cerebrum
questions.question: The cavities inside the cerebrum filled with CSF are named:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The central canal is the narrow, CSF-filled channel running through the spinal cord, not the cavities inside the cerebrum.
explanations.B: Correct. The brain's CSF-filled cavities are its four ventricles. These are the two lateral ventricles (one per cerebral hemisphere), the third ventricle (diencephalon) and the fourth ventricle (between the pons/medulla and cerebellum). All four are filled with, and connected by, circulating CSF.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cisterns are subarachnoid CSF pools outside the brain substance, distinct from the ventricles inside it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lacunae are not a recognised CSF space of the brain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Venous sinuses carry venous blood, not CSF, and are not cavities within the brain substance.

questions.learning_objective: Name the ventricles as the brain's CSF-filled cavities, distinct from cisterns and sinuses.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.25

questions.title: Example of a major cerebral sulcus
questions.question: The one major sulcus among the following is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The precentral sulcus is a minor, variable fold in front of the precentral gyrus, not one of the four constant, named landmark sulci.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The postcentral sulcus is likewise a minor, variable fold, behind the postcentral gyrus, not a constant landmark sulcus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The collateral sulcus is a minor temporal-lobe fold, not one of the brain's constant landmark sulci.
explanations.D: Correct. Only a handful of sulci are constant enough across individuals to serve as fixed landmarks: the central, lateral, parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. The calcarine sulcus, on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, marks the primary visual cortex.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Preoccipital is a notch, not a named constant sulcus, on the lateral surface near the occipital lobe's boundary.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the calcarine sulcus as one of the brain's few constant, named landmark sulci.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.25

questions.author_notes: The source's own stem ("the one major sulcus") implies uniqueness the fact does not have, since four sulci (central, lateral, parieto-occipital, calcarine) are equally constant landmarks; rephrased to "the one major sulcus among the following" and authored against the printed key, with the fuller set given in the concept/article.

questions.title: What an axo-somatic synapse connects
questions.question: The axo-somatic synapse is best described as the meeting between an axon and:

options.B: The cell body of another neuron
options.D: An effector organ, such as muscle or gland

explanations.A: Incorrect. An axon terminal meeting another neuron's dendrites is an axo-dendritic synapse, not an axo-somatic one.
explanations.B: Correct. Synapses are named by what the presynaptic axon terminal meets. An axo-somatic synapse specifically meets the cell body (soma) of the next neuron, which is what the prefix "somatic" in its name identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An axon terminal meeting another neuron's axon is an axo-axonic synapse, a different type from the one named in the question.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An axon terminal meeting a muscle fibre is the motor end plate, a specialised junction with its own name rather than one of the three axo- synapse types.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A synapse connects one excitable cell to another; it does not meet an empty cavity.

questions.learning_objective: Define an axo-somatic synapse as the meeting between an axon terminal and another neuron's cell body.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.25

questions.title: What the motor end plate connects
questions.question: The motor end plate is the meeting between an axon and:

options.B: The cell body of another neuron

explanations.A: Incorrect. An axon meeting another neuron's dendrites is an axo-dendritic synapse, a neuron-to-neuron contact, not the motor end plate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An axon meeting another neuron's cell body is an axo-somatic synapse, also a neuron-to-neuron contact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An axon meeting another neuron's axon is an axo-axonic synapse, again a neuron-to-neuron contact rather than a nerve-to-muscle one.
explanations.D: Correct. The motor end plate is the specialised junction where a motor axon terminal meets a skeletal muscle fibre, separated from it by a synaptic cleft rich in acetylcholinesterase. Because the contact is with muscle rather than with another neuron, it is given its own name rather than being classed as one of the three axo- synapse types.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The motor end plate is a structured junction with a muscle fibre, not a meeting with an empty cavity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the motor end plate as the junction between a motor axon terminal and a muscle fibre.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.25

questions.title: Characteristic sympathetic nervous system effect
questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of sympathetic nervous system functions?

options.B: Excitatory to everything except the heart
options.C: Increases glandular secretion and peristalsis of the gut

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Rest and digest" describes the parasympathetic system's overall action, the opposite of the sympathetic "fight and flight" pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the sympathetic system that is inhibitory to everything except the heart, not excitatory; the heart is the one organ excited by both divisions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing glandular secretion and gut peristalsis is a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic activity instead decreases them.
explanations.D: Correct. Sympathetic activity contracts the sphincters, part of its overall inhibitory effect on the gut, alongside decreased glandular secretion and peristalsis and bronchodilatation. Parasympathetic activity relaxes the sphincters instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bronchoconstriction is a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic activity instead produces bronchodilatation.

questions.learning_objective: State that sympathetic activity contracts the sphincters, part of its inhibitory effect on the gut.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.25

questions.title: Part of the spinal nerve containing sensory fibres only
questions.question: Which one of the following parts of a spinal nerve contains sensory fibres ONLY?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal ramus is a branch of the already-united, mixed spinal nerve trunk, so it carries both sensory and motor fibres, not sensory fibres only.
explanations.B: Correct. The dorsal (posterior) root carries sensory (afferent) fibres only, before it unites with the ventral root to form the mixed spinal nerve trunk. It also bears the dorsal root ganglion, where the sensory neuron cell bodies lie.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spinal nerve trunk forms only after the dorsal and ventral roots unite, and is therefore already a mixed nerve carrying both sensory and motor fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ventral ramus, like the dorsal ramus, is a branch of the mixed nerve trunk and so carries both sensory and motor fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ventral (anterior) root carries motor (efferent) fibres only, the opposite of the sensory-only root asked for here.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dorsal root, before its union with the ventral root, carries sensory fibres only.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: Where a ganglion is found
questions.question: The ganglion is a collection of nerve cells at which of the following sites?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A collection of nerve cell bodies inside the cerebellum is not termed a ganglion; the cerebellum's own neuron cell bodies (such as Purkinje cells) are part of the CNS.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A collection of nerve cell bodies inside the cerebrum is a nucleus, not a ganglion, since the cerebrum is part of the CNS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A collection of nerve cell bodies inside the spinal cord, such as its grey matter, is likewise called a nucleus, not a ganglion, again because it lies within the CNS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The meninges are protective membranous coverings of the brain and spinal cord; nerve cell bodies are not grouped there.
explanations.E: Correct. A ganglion is specifically an aggregation of nerve cell bodies outside the central nervous system, in the peripheral nervous system, such as a dorsal root or autonomic ganglion. The equivalent grouping inside the CNS is instead called a nucleus.

questions.learning_objective: Define a ganglion as a collection of nerve cell bodies outside the CNS, distinct from a nucleus inside it.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: Cranial nerve arising outside the brainstem
questions.question: Which one of the following cranial nerves arises from outside the brainstem?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The facial nerve's nucleus lies in the pons, part of the brainstem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve's nucleus lies in the medulla, part of the brainstem.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve's nucleus lies in the midbrain, part of the brainstem.
explanations.D: Correct. The optic nerve develops as an outgrowth of the diencephalon, not of the midbrain, pons or medulla. This makes it one of only two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem. The olfactory nerve, an extension of the forebrain, is the other exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The vagus nerve's nucleus lies in the medulla, part of the brainstem.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the optic nerve as a cranial nerve that arises outside the brainstem, from the diencephalon.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: Example of a peripheral neuroglia cell
questions.question: Which one of the following is a peripheral neuroglia cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Astrocytes are a central (CNS) neuroglial cell, supporting neurons and helping form the blood-brain barrier.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ependymal cells are a central (CNS) neuroglial cell, lining the ventricles and central canal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Microglia are a central (CNS) neuroglial cell, acting as the resident phagocytes of the brain and spinal cord.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oligodendrocytes are a central (CNS) neuroglial cell, myelinating axons within the brain and spinal cord.
explanations.E: Correct. Satellite cells are a peripheral neuroglial cell, surrounding and supporting the cell bodies of neurons within a ganglion, such as a dorsal root or autonomic ganglion. Schwann cells are the peripheral nervous system's other neuroglial cell, myelinating peripheral axons instead.

questions.learning_objective: Identify satellite cells as the peripheral neuroglial cell that supports ganglion neuron cell bodies.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: Location of synaptic vesicles
questions.question: Synaptic vesicles are present in the:

explanations.A: Correct. Synaptic vesicles, which store the presynaptic neuron's neurotransmitter, cluster in the axon terminal, immediately adjacent to the synaptic cleft. An arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels there, and the calcium influx triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dendrites are typically the postsynaptic element receiving a signal, carrying receptors rather than the presynaptic vesicles that release neurotransmitter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The postsynaptic element carries neurotransmitter receptors, not the vesicles that store and release neurotransmitter, which belong to the presynaptic side.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The synaptic cleft is the fluid-filled gap the released neurotransmitter crosses; it is empty space, not a storage site for vesicles.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nerve cell body is where the neurotransmitter's components are synthesised, but the finished vesicles are transported to and concentrated in the axon terminal, not held in bulk at the cell body.

questions.learning_objective: Locate synaptic vesicles in the axon terminal, not the postsynaptic element or synaptic cleft.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: Number of thoracic spinal nerves
questions.question: The number of the thoracic spinal nerves is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Five is the count of lumbar spinal nerve pairs, not thoracic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Six is not one of the spinal cord's regional segment counts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eight is the count of cervical spinal nerve pairs, not thoracic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ten is not one of the spinal cord's regional segment counts.
explanations.E: Correct. There are 12 pairs of thoracic spinal nerves. This count matches the 12 thoracic vertebrae exactly, unlike the cervical region, where the nerve count (8) exceeds the vertebral count (7). The thoracic region is therefore the simpler one to remember, since nerve and vertebra numbers line up one-to-one.

questions.learning_objective: State that there are 12 pairs of thoracic spinal nerves, matching the 12 thoracic vertebrae.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: Brainstem levels of the parasympathetic cranial outflow
questions.question: Cranial outflow of the parasympathetic nervous system arises from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The midbrain contributes the oculomotor nerve (III) to the cranial outflow, but this is only one of the three levels involved, not the outflow's sole source.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pons contributes the facial nerve (VII), again only one of the three levels involved.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The medulla contributes the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves, but this too is only part of the outflow, not its sole source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Naming midbrain and medulla omits the pons, which also contributes via the facial nerve (VII).
explanations.E: Correct. The parasympathetic cranial outflow leaves the brainstem at all three levels together. The midbrain contributes via cranial nerve III, the pons via VII, and the medulla via IX and X. No single level carries the outflow on its own.

questions.learning_objective: State that the parasympathetic cranial outflow leaves the brainstem at all three levels (midbrain, pons, medulla), not just one.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: Parts of the central nervous system
questions.question: What are the parts of the central nervous system (CNS)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The peripheral and autonomic nervous systems are functional/anatomical divisions that run through, or lie outside, the CNS; they are not themselves the parts the CNS is made of.
explanations.B: Correct. The central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord. Both are protected within bone, the brain by the skull and the spinal cord by the vertebral column. Everything that connects this pair to the rest of the body belongs instead to the peripheral nervous system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cranial nerves are part of the peripheral nervous system, not the CNS, so pairing the brain with cranial nerves mixes the two compartments.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cranial nerves and spinal nerves together make up the peripheral nervous system, not the CNS.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spinal nerves are peripheral structures; pairing the spinal cord (CNS) with spinal nerves (PNS) again mixes the two compartments.

questions.learning_objective: State that the CNS is composed of the brain and spinal cord.

questions.title: Function of ependymal cells
questions.question: Ependymal cells are best described by which of the following?

options.C: Acting as the CNS's resident phagocyte
options.E: Lining the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord

explanations.A: Incorrect. Forming the blood-brain barrier is the astrocyte's role, not the ependymal cell's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myelinating axons within the CNS is the oligodendrocyte's role, not the ependymal cell's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acting as the CNS's resident phagocyte is the microglial cell's role, not the ependymal cell's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Surrounding ganglion neuron cell bodies is the peripheral satellite cell's role, not a CNS ependymal cell's.
explanations.E: Correct. Ependymal cells are ciliated or cuboidal cells that line the CSF-filled cavities of the CNS. This lining covers both the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. Their beating cilia also contribute to circulating the CSF within these cavities.

questions.learning_objective: State that ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.

field_notes.keySource: printed short answer, p.29

questions.title: Composition of the peripheral nervous system
questions.question: Which of the following makes up the peripheral nervous system?

explanations.A: Correct. The peripheral nervous system is everything outside the CNS that connects it to the rest of the body. It comprises the twelve pairs of cranial nerves and the thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves, together with the ganglia that lie along them. The brain and spinal cord themselves are not part of this peripheral compartment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The brain and spinal cord together make up the central nervous system, not the peripheral nervous system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are a functional subdivision running through both the CNS and PNS, not the whole of the PNS by themselves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The brain is part of the CNS, not the PNS, so pairing it with cranial nerves mixes the two compartments.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The spinal cord is part of the CNS, not the PNS.

questions.learning_objective: State that the PNS is composed of the cranial nerves and spinal nerves.
